topic.name: Deep Learning
topic.description: Neural representations, computational graphs, and gradient-based optimization.

concepts.name: Gradient-based optimization
concepts.description: Iterative optimization driven by local derivatives, curvature, conditioning, and step-size choices.

concepts.name: Neural networks
concepts.description: Compositions of parameterized differentiable transformations that learn representations.

concepts.name: Backpropagation and computational graphs
concepts.description: Reverse-mode differentiation through a computational graph, including explicit gradient stops.

concepts.name: Representation learning
concepts.description: Learning features that make relevant structure usable by downstream tasks.

misconceptions.name: A tiny learning rate fixes conditioning
misconceptions.description: Confuses stable steps with efficient progress when curvature differs greatly by direction.
misconceptions.remediation: Analyze convergence along the largest and smallest Hessian eigen-directions.

misconceptions.name: More iterations improve the condition number
misconceptions.description: Treats a geometric property of the objective as if it changes merely by running the same optimizer longer.
misconceptions.remediation: Distinguish modifying the objective geometry from traversing it for more steps.

misconceptions.name: Momentum guarantees perfect conditioning
misconceptions.description: Overstates acceleration and assumes momentum removes all sensitivity to curvature and scaling.
misconceptions.remediation: Treat momentum as an optimizer choice, not an algebraic transformation to condition number one.

misconceptions.name: Stop-gradient blocks downstream parameter updates
misconceptions.description: Assumes detaching an intermediate value prevents later layers from receiving gradients from their own operations.
misconceptions.remediation: Trace local derivatives backward edge by edge and mark only the detached edge as zero.

misconceptions.name: Forward use guarantees gradient flow
misconceptions.description: Assumes any parameter that influences a forward value must receive a gradient even across an explicit detach operation.
misconceptions.remediation: Separate forward dependence from differentiable backward connectivity.

misconceptions.name: Stop-gradient changes values but not derivatives
misconceptions.description: Reverses the operation: detach preserves the forward value precisely while replacing one backward derivative with zero.
misconceptions.remediation: Write the stop-gradient operator as identity in the forward pass and zero derivative in the backward pass.

misconceptions.name: Depth alone creates nonlinear expressivity
misconceptions.description: Assumes stacking affine layers without nonlinear activations yields functions beyond a single affine transformation.
misconceptions.remediation: Compose two affine maps algebraically and identify the activation that prevents their collapse.

misconceptions.name: Universal approximation guarantees successful training
misconceptions.description: Treats an existence result for representable functions as a guarantee that finite data and an optimizer will find a useful solution.
misconceptions.remediation: Separate representational capacity from optimization, sample efficiency, and out-of-sample validation.

misconceptions.name: Hidden units have fixed human meanings
misconceptions.description: Assumes each learned coordinate has an intrinsic, uniquely identifiable semantic interpretation across equivalent parameterizations.
misconceptions.remediation: Apply a permutation of hidden units and the inverse permutation to the next layer while observing unchanged predictions.

misconceptions.name: The most lossless representation is always best
misconceptions.description: Ranks representations only by retained input detail even when nuisance variation harms the downstream task.
misconceptions.remediation: Compare representations using held-out task utility and robustness to known nuisance changes.

misconceptions.name: Representation dimension determines utility
misconceptions.description: Infers downstream usefulness solely from the number of coordinates rather than the information and invariances they encode.
misconceptions.remediation: Hold dimension fixed while changing the learned objective, then compare downstream separability and robustness.

misconceptions.name: Pretraining guarantees transfer
misconceptions.description: Assumes success on a source pretraining objective necessarily improves every target task and domain.
misconceptions.remediation: Measure target-task performance under a deployment-aligned split and compare frozen, fine-tuned, and baseline representations.

questions.stem: Gradient descent on a convex quadratic loss zigzags along a steep direction but advances very slowly along a shallow direction. The Hessian has a large ratio between its largest and smallest eigenvalues. Which intervention most directly addresses the cause?

options.text: Rescale, whiten, or precondition the coordinates to improve the condition number, then retune the step size.
options.rationale: The pathology is anisotropic curvature; a coordinate transformation or preconditioner directly makes progress more even across directions.

options.text: Use an extremely small learning rate; once oscillation stops, convergence is equally fast in all eigendirections.
options.rationale: A smaller step can stabilize the steep direction but makes progress along the shallow direction even slower.

options.text: Run the same update longer, because repeated gradients gradually reduce the Hessian's condition number.
options.rationale: For a fixed quadratic, the Hessian and its condition number do not improve merely because more iterations are executed.

options.text: Add momentum with any coefficient; momentum algebraically changes the quadratic to condition number one.
options.rationale: Momentum may accelerate a tuned optimization but neither guarantees perfect conditioning nor removes the need to respect curvature.

questions.stem: A computation is h = f_theta(x), z = stop_gradient(h), prediction = g_phi(z), followed by a scalar loss. Neither parameter set is used elsewhere. What happens during backpropagation?

options.text: Neither theta nor phi receives a gradient, because detaching z disconnects everything after h from the loss.
options.rationale: The loss remains differentiably connected to phi through g; only the backward edge from z to h is blocked.

options.text: Phi receives its ordinary gradient, while theta receives zero through this path; the forward value of z still equals h.
options.rationale: Stop-gradient is identity in the forward pass and has zero derivative at the detached edge in the backward pass.

options.text: Theta receives a gradient because h influenced the prediction value, while phi receives none because z is treated as constant.
options.rationale: Forward influence does not cross a detached backward edge, whereas treating z as constant still permits differentiation with respect to phi.

options.text: Both parameter sets update normally because stop_gradient modifies the forward tensor value but leaves its derivative unchanged.
options.rationale: This reverses the operator's definition: its value is unchanged, but its derivative toward h is set to zero.

questions.stem: A feed-forward network computes h = W1 x + b1 and y = W2 h + b2, with no activation or other nonlinear operation between the two layers. Relative to a single affine layer, what function class does this network represent?

options.text: A strictly richer nonlinear class, because two learned layers create depth even without an activation.
options.rationale: Depth alone does not prevent affine maps from composing into another affine map.

options.text: The same affine class, since y = (W2 W1)x + (W2 b1 + b2) can be represented by one layer.
options.rationale: Substitution collapses the composition to one matrix and one bias; nonlinear activations change that conclusion.

options.text: A class with guaranteed learnability, because a sufficiently wide hidden layer ensures the optimizer finds its best parameters.
options.rationale: Width and representability do not supply an optimization guarantee, and the stated network remains affine.

options.text: A uniquely interpretable class, because each coordinate of h identifies one stable human-readable feature.
options.rationale: Hidden coordinates can be reparameterized without changing the represented input-output function.

questions.stem: A theorem says a sufficiently wide network can approximate any continuous function on a compact domain to arbitrary accuracy. A team cites it as proof that its training run will learn the correct deployment function. What is missing?

options.text: An argument that extra depth itself makes the learned mapping nonlinear even if the configured activations are removed.
options.rationale: This changes the architecture question but does not bridge an approximation existence theorem to learning.

options.text: A mapping from each hidden coordinate to a fixed semantic concept shared by all equivalent parameter settings.
options.rationale: Unit-level semantic uniqueness is not required for prediction and is not supplied by approximation capacity.

options.text: Evidence about optimization, finite-sample identification, regularization, and held-out performance under the deployment distribution.
options.rationale: Representability is an existence statement; learning also depends on data, search, inductive bias, and external validation.

options.text: A larger hidden layer, because universal approximation means added width directly proves that gradient training reaches a useful solution.
options.rationale: Increasing capacity does not turn an existence result into convergence or generalization evidence.

questions.stem: In a one-hidden-layer network, the hidden units are permuted and the corresponding input columns of the next layer are permuted inversely. Activations and all numeric weights otherwise stay the same. What happens?

options.text: The network becomes affine because reordering hidden coordinates removes the nonlinear effect of its activations.
options.rationale: A coordinate permutation does not remove or linearize the activation function.

options.text: The network gains a convergence advantage because the permutation selects an equivalent minimum with better training properties.
options.rationale: Equivalence of parameterizations does not establish how an optimizer reaches either one.

options.text: Predictions change because each hidden unit has a fixed semantic identity tied to its original coordinate.
options.rationale: The compensating permutation demonstrates that unit indices are not uniquely identified by the input-output function.

options.text: Predictions remain unchanged because the inverse permutation restores the same weighted combination at the next layer.
options.rationale: The hidden vector is reindexed and then reindexed back in the downstream linear map, leaving the function invariant.

questions.stem: For recognizing manufactured parts, representation A preserves exact lighting and background pixels, while representation B discards those variations but separates part geometry. On held-out factory lines, B yields better recognition. Which conclusion is strongest?

options.text: B is more useful for this task because its invariances suppress nuisance detail while preserving geometry that transfers across lines.
options.rationale: Representation quality is relative to task-relevant information and deployment variation, not raw detail retention alone.

options.text: A is more useful because the representation retaining the most input information is preferable for downstream prediction.
options.rationale: Preserving nuisance information can make a downstream predictor less robust even when reconstruction is excellent.

options.text: The comparison is settled by whichever representation has more coordinates, independent of what those coordinates encode.
options.rationale: Dimension alone does not say whether the coordinates expose geometry or background artifacts.

options.text: A pretraining objective selecting either representation establishes its benefit on new lines without a held-out recognition test.
options.rationale: Source-objective performance does not substitute for evaluation on the intended target task and domain.

questions.stem: Two encoders each map an image to 128 numbers. A linear probe separates disease status well from encoder X but remains near chance for encoder Y on a patient-grouped test set. What does this comparison establish?

options.text: Y is preferable if it reconstructs more pixel detail, because retained information dominates the downstream probe result.
options.rationale: Reconstruction may preserve irrelevant variation while failing to expose disease information to the chosen downstream model.

options.text: At equal dimension, X makes disease-relevant structure more usable by this probe under the tested patient-level deployment split.
options.rationale: The controlled dimension and held-out probe provide task-specific evidence about accessibility of relevant information.

options.text: The encoders are equivalent because equal vector length fixes the amount and organization of useful information.
options.rationale: Equal coordinate count permits very different information, geometry, and invariances.

options.text: Whichever encoder used pretraining should be preferred because source-objective learning establishes transfer to disease status.
options.rationale: Pretraining is a hypothesis about transfer; the deployment-aligned probe supplies the relevant comparative evidence.

questions.stem: An encoder pretrained to identify camera models transfers poorly to classifying plant disease because it emphasizes sensor artifacts. A smaller encoder trained for leaf morphology performs better on farms using unseen cameras. What lesson is best supported?

options.text: The larger encoder remains preferable because preserving sensor-specific detail makes a representation more complete for later tasks.
options.rationale: Retaining source-specific nuisance detail can damage robustness to the target camera change.

options.text: The larger encoder remains preferable because more coordinates determine greater utility independent of learned invariances.
options.rationale: Capacity or dimensionality does not ensure that target-relevant factors are encoded accessibly.

options.text: Transfer depends on alignment between learned factors and the target variation, so pretraining success needs target-domain validation.
options.rationale: The result is negative transfer: a source-useful representation emphasizes variation that is spurious for the target.

options.text: Camera-model pretraining establishes target usefulness because a successful source objective carries over to downstream tasks.
options.rationale: The scenario directly shows that source success can encode the wrong invariances for a new task.

questions.stem: A shared activation h = f_theta(x) feeds two losses: L1(g_phi(h)) and L2(k_psi(stop_gradient(h))). The total loss is L1 + L2. Which gradient routing is correct?

options.text: L2 stops updates to psi because detaching its input blocks gradients for operations downstream of h.
options.rationale: Psi still affects L2 after the detach and receives gradients through its own downstream computation.

options.text: Both losses update theta because h appears in both forward computations and forward use determines gradient flow.
options.rationale: The explicit stop-gradient removes the derivative path from L2 back into theta.

options.text: L1 updates theta and phi; L2 updates psi but contributes no gradient to theta through its detached input.
options.rationale: Detach preserves the forward value for k while replacing the backward derivative from that branch to h with zero.

options.text: L2 changes the forward activation passed to k while preserving its derivative path back into theta.
options.rationale: Stop-gradient has the opposite semantics: same forward value, blocked derivative at the boundary.

questions.stem: A loss is ||p_theta(x) - stop_gradient(t_phi(x))|| squared. During this update, theta and phi are distinct parameter sets and phi is used nowhere else. What parameter update follows from automatic differentiation?

options.text: Phi is updated but theta is not, because stop-gradient blocks parameters downstream from the target value.
options.rationale: Theta lies on the live prediction path; phi lies behind the detached target boundary.

options.text: Both theta and phi are updated because both parameter sets influence values used in the forward loss.
options.rationale: Forward influence does not overcome the explicit derivative stop around t_phi.

options.text: Phi is updated through an unchanged derivative while its target values are replaced during the forward pass.
options.rationale: The target value is preserved in the forward pass and the gradient into phi is removed.

options.text: Theta receives the prediction-error gradient, while phi receives no gradient from this loss during the stated update.
options.rationale: The live branch differentiates through p_theta; the detached target acts as a constant for this backward pass.

questions.stem: For loss L = 100 x squared + y squared, ordinary gradient descent uses one learning rate and zigzags in x while progressing slowly in y. Which change most directly improves the coordinate conditioning?

options.text: Use a much smaller shared learning rate, which makes progress efficient by removing the curvature ratio.
options.rationale: A smaller step can stabilize x but leaves the 100-to-1 curvature ratio and slow y progress.

options.text: Run more iterations with the same coordinates, which improves the Hessian condition number over optimization time.
options.rationale: The Hessian of this fixed quadratic and its condition number do not change merely because iterations pass.

options.text: Rescale or precondition the coordinates so gradient steps account for their different curvature scales.
options.rationale: A suitable coordinate scaling makes the level sets more isotropic and permits balanced progress.

options.text: Add momentum and infer that curvature sensitivity has been removed, independent of its tuning.
options.rationale: Momentum may accelerate a tuned problem but does not make the objective perfectly conditioned.

questions.stem: A learning rate is reduced until gradient descent no longer diverges on an ill-conditioned objective, but loss then decreases extremely slowly. Which statement best distinguishes stability from efficiency?

options.text: The small step has repaired conditioning because a stable trajectory implies similar progress along all curvature directions.
options.rationale: Stability in the steep direction can coexist with very slow movement in shallow directions.

options.text: Continuing the same iterations will improve the objective's condition number and eventually balance the coordinate speeds.
options.rationale: The local curvature ratio is a property of the objective and parameterization, not elapsed iteration count.

options.text: Adding momentum makes efficiency independent of curvature, so tuning and scaling no longer matter.
options.rationale: Momentum remains sensitive to hyperparameters and the curvature spectrum even when it improves convergence.

options.text: The step is stable but inefficient; scaling, preconditioning, or a suitable adaptive method can address directional imbalance.
options.rationale: Avoiding divergence is a weaker property than making useful progress across both steep and shallow directions.

questions.stem: Encoder A has lower pretraining loss, twice as many output coordinates, and strong scanner-ID information. Encoder B performs better on disease classification across held-out hospitals. Which evidence should drive selection?

options.text: Choose A because preserving scanner detail makes the more lossless representation preferable for the disease task.
options.rationale: Scanner information is a nuisance under hospital shift and can harm the deployment-aligned target task.

options.text: Choose A because its larger coordinate count determines that it contains the more useful downstream representation.
options.rationale: Dimension alone does not reveal which target-relevant information and invariances the coordinates encode.

options.text: Choose A because lower source pretraining loss establishes improved transfer to the hospital distribution.
options.rationale: Source-objective success does not establish target utility under a different domain and grouping structure.

options.text: Prefer B based on the hospital-grouped target evaluation, while retaining uncertainty until broader deployment checks confirm the result.
options.rationale: Deployment-aligned held-out performance directly tests the desired transfer and robustness better than proxy size or source loss.

questions.stem: Let x = 3, theta = 2, h = theta x, z = stop_gradient(h), y = phi z with phi = 5, and L = one half y squared. What gradients does reverse-mode automatic differentiation produce?

options.text: Theta receives 450 and phi receives 180, because both forward dependencies are treated as differentiable backward paths.
options.rationale: The numerical derivatives are those of the graph without a detached edge; forward dependence by itself does not preserve that edge.

options.text: Theta receives zero and phi receives 180, because z keeps the value 6 but is constant with respect to theta.
options.rationale: The live derivative is dL/dphi = y z = 30 times 6, while the detached z-to-h derivative removes this loss's path to theta.

options.text: Theta and phi both receive zero, because detaching h also blocks differentiation of operations that consume z.
options.rationale: Phi remains downstream of the detached value and directly changes y, so its local derivative is still active.

options.text: Phi receives zero because z becomes zero, while theta receives 450 because the backward derivative through h remains live.
options.rationale: This reverses both semantics: stop-gradient preserves z's forward value and removes the derivative entering h.

questions.stem: A program defines q(x) = round(x) and y = x + stop_gradient(q(x) - x). At x = 3.2, which forward value and local automatic-differentiation derivative dy/dx should a debugger observe?

options.text: The forward value is 3.2 and the derivative follows q'(x), because detaching changes the value but preserves the enclosed derivative.
options.rationale: Stop-gradient does the reverse: the enclosed expression retains its forward value while its derivative contribution is removed.

options.text: The forward value is 3 and the derivative is zero, because the detached term blocks gradients for the complete downstream expression.
options.rationale: The separate leading x remains a live differentiable path even though the correction term is detached.

options.text: The forward value is 3 and the derivative follows q'(x), because q determines the output value in the forward computation.
options.rationale: A value can determine the forward result while residing behind an explicit zero-derivative boundary.

options.text: The forward value is 3 and the derivative is one, because the detached correction supplies rounding while the leading x supplies the gradient.
options.rationale: Forward evaluation gives x plus q(x) minus x, while automatic differentiation sees derivative one plus zero from the detached correction.

questions.stem: A least-squares model has Hessian eigenvalues 81 and 1. Gradient descent uses eta = 1/81, so an error component with eigenvalue lambda is multiplied by 1 - eta lambda each step. Which diagnosis is correct?

options.text: Both eigendirections now converge at comparable rates, because a stable small step removes the curvature imbalance.
options.rationale: Stability in the steep coordinate does not make progress in the shallow coordinate comparably fast.

options.text: Once the steep-direction error reaches zero, later iterations change the Hessian condition number from 81 to one.
options.rationale: The fixed least-squares Hessian retains eigenvalues 81 and one regardless of the current error vector.

options.text: The steep multiplier is zero and the shallow multiplier is 80/81, so stability coexists with unchanged ill-conditioning.
options.rationale: Substitution gives immediate contraction in the steep component and very slow contraction in the shallow one, while the condition number stays 81.

options.text: Adding a momentum coefficient makes the Hessian condition number one, independent of the selected coefficient.
options.rationale: Momentum changes the update dynamics but does not algebraically replace the objective's curvature spectrum.

questions.stem: For one Hessian eigen-direction, heavy-ball error follows e_(t+1) = (1 + beta - eta lambda)e_t - beta e_(t-1), whose characteristic polynomial is r^2 - (1 + beta - eta lambda)r + beta. With beta = 0.5, eta = 0.0375, and Hessian eigenvalues 20 and 100, which spectral calculation and response are correct?

options.text: At lambda = 20 the roots have modulus sqrt(0.5), but at lambda = 100 they are -2 and -0.25 with radius 2; a positive eta below 0.03 restores stability without changing conditioning.
options.rationale: At lambda = 20 the polynomial has a complex-conjugate pair with product 0.5. At lambda = 100 it is r^2 + 2.25r + 0.5; the endpoint condition eta lambda < 2(1 + beta) requires eta < 0.03.

options.text: At lambda = 100 the root -2 will move inside the unit circle after enough iterations, because continuing the recurrence gradually improves the Hessian condition number.
options.rationale: The characteristic roots and the fixed Hessian spectrum do not change with iteration count; a root of magnitude 2 amplifies error.

options.text: Reducing eta below 0.03 makes the lambda = 20 and lambda = 100 directions equally conditioned, so the smaller step removes the curvature ratio as well as the instability.
options.rationale: A smaller step can place both recurrences in the stable region, but it does not alter the eigenvalue ratio 100/20.

options.text: Because the product of the two roots is beta = 0.5, both directions have spectral radius sqrt(0.5); momentum makes their curvature equivalent even when the roots are real.
options.rationale: A fixed root product implies equal moduli only for a complex-conjugate pair; the lambda = 100 roots are real with maximum magnitude 2.

questions.stem: A one-hidden-layer network is y(x) = v^T ReLU(Wx + b). At x0, the two hidden preactivations are (-2, 3), their directional changes along u are Wu = (5, -4), and v = (7, 2). For a sufficiently small positive step that crosses neither ReLU boundary, what is D_u y(x0), and what does this local result establish?

options.text: D_u y(x0) = -8; the inactive first unit contributes zero and the network is affine within this activation region, without establishing a global training result.
options.rationale: The fixed local ReLU mask is diag(0, 1), so v^T diag(0, 1)Wu = 7(0) + 2(-4) = -8.

options.text: No single derivative is determined: retaining input-to-hidden and hidden-to-output layers makes the local function more expressive than one affine map even when the activation mask is fixed.
options.rationale: Once the activation signs are fixed, the ReLU mask is linear and the composed local map has a directly computable affine derivative.

options.text: D_u y(x0) = 27; the first hidden coordinate's learned semantic role means its directional change 5 contributes even while its preactivation is negative.
options.rationale: A coordinate label cannot override the ReLU gate: the negative preactivation makes that unit's local derivative zero.

options.text: D_u y(x0) = -8, and this local derivative proves that sufficient hidden width ensures an optimizer will learn the desired global function from finite data.
options.rationale: A correct local derivative calculation says nothing by itself about optimizer convergence, finite-sample generalization, or global approximation quality.

questions.stem: One hidden ReLU unit contributes v ReLU(w transpose x + b) to a network output. Its incoming w and b are multiplied by positive alpha = 10 while v is divided by 10. What follows from ReLU's positive homogeneity?

options.text: The output changes because the hidden unit's original magnitude fixes its semantic identity within the network.
options.rationale: The compensating rescaling is a function-preserving parameter symmetry, so unit scale is not a uniquely identified semantic quantity.

options.text: The unit becomes affine because compensating adjacent weights removes the nonlinear effect of its ReLU.
options.rationale: Positive rescaling preserves the ReLU operation and its activation boundary rather than replacing it with an identity.

options.text: The rescaled parameters improve optimization by theorem, because representational capacity establishes how training reaches a useful solution.
options.rationale: Function equivalence and approximation capacity do not establish that one parameter scale has better training dynamics.

options.text: The network function is unchanged, although parameter magnitudes and Euclidean geometry can change under the equivalent representation.
options.rationale: For positive alpha, ReLU(alpha z) = alpha ReLU(z), which is canceled by dividing the outgoing coefficient by alpha.

questions.stem: Contrastive pretraining for microscopy treats large stain-color changes as positive pairs. Stain color is partly diagnostic for the downstream assay, and the resulting encoder has low pretraining loss but worse lab-held-out assay accuracy. What is the strongest next step?

options.text: Switch to the encoder with highest reconstruction fidelity, because retaining more input detail settles downstream representation quality.
options.rationale: High-fidelity reconstruction may retain nuisance detail and does not establish which information the assay needs.

options.text: Increase the embedding dimension, because coordinate count determines whether stain information is useful for the assay.
options.rationale: More coordinates do not repair an objective that explicitly trains away target-relevant variation.

options.text: Revisit which augmentations are label-preserving, then compare candidate objectives on lab-held-out target performance and stain-shift diagnostics.
options.rationale: Contrastive positives induce invariances, so augmentation semantics must align with the target before deployment-aligned evaluation can support selection.

options.text: Keep the lower-loss encoder, because success on its pretraining objective establishes transfer to the downstream assay.
options.rationale: The observed target degradation is direct evidence that source-objective success did not establish beneficial transfer.
